title: github/copilot-cli — GitHub Copilot CLI brings the power of Copilot coding agent directly to your terminal.
content:
The power of GitHub Copilot, now in your terminal.
GitHub Copilot CLI brings AI-powered coding assistance directly to your command line, enabling you to build, debug, and understand code through natural language conversations. Powered by the same agentic harness as GitHub's Copilot coding agent, it provides intelligent assistance while staying deeply integrated with your GitHub workflow.
See our official documentation for more information.
We're bringing the power of GitHub Copilot coding agent directly to your terminal. With GitHub Copilot CLI, you can work locally and synchronously with an AI agent that understands your code and GitHub context.
- Terminal-native development: Work with Copilot coding agent directly in your command line — no context switching required.
- GitHub integration out of the box: Access your repositories, issues, and pull requests using natural language, all authenticated with your existing GitHub account.
- Agentic capabilities: Build, edit, debug, and refactor code with an AI collaborator that can plan and execute complex tasks.
- MCP-powered extensibility: Take advantage of the fact that the coding agent ships with GitHub's MCP server by default and supports custom MCP servers to extend capabilities.
- Full control: Preview every action before execution — nothing happens without your explicit approval.
We're still early in our journey, but with your feedback, we're rapidly iterating to make the GitHub Copilot CLI the best possible companion in your terminal.
- Linux
- macOS
- Windows
- (On Windows) PowerShell v6 or higher
- An active Copilot subscription. See Copilot plans.
If you have access to GitHub Copilot via your organization or enterprise, you cannot use GitHub Copilot CLI if your organization owner or enterprise administrator has disabled it in the organization or enterprise settings. See Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization for more information.
Install with the install script (macOS and Linux):
curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash
Or
wget -qO- https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash
Use | sudo bash to run as root and install to /usr/local/bin.
Set PREFIX to install to $PREFIX/bin/ directory. Defaults to /usr/local
when run as root or $HOME/.local when run as a non-root user.
Set VERSION to install a specific version. Defaults to the latest version.
For example, to install version v0.0.369 to a custom directory:
curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | VERSION="v0.0.369" PREFIX="$HOME/custom" bash
Install with Homebrew (macOS and Linux):
brew install copilot-clibrew install copilot-cli@prerelease
Install with WinGet (Windows):
winget install GitHub.Copilotwinget install GitHub.Copilot.Prerelease
Install with npm (macOS, Linux, and Windows):
npm install -g @github/copilotnpm install -g @github/copilot@prereleasecopilot
On first launch, you'll be greeted with our adorable animated banner! If you'd like to see this banner again, launch copilot with the --banner flag.
If you're not currently logged in to GitHub, you'll be prompted to use the /login slash command. Enter this command and follow the on-screen instructions to authenticate.
You can also authenticate using a fine-grained PAT with the "Copilot Requests" permission enabled.
- Visit https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new
- Under "Permissions," click "add permissions" and select "Copilot Requests"
- Generate your token
- Add the token to your environment via the environment variable GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN (in order of precedence)
Launch copilot in a folder that contains code you want to work with.
By default, copilot utilizes Claude Sonnet 4.5. Run the /model slash command to choose from other available models, including Claude Sonnet 4 and GPT-5.
The Copilot CLI is also available as a container image that runs the CLI as a headless server for Copilot SDK clients. Images are published to ghcr.io/github/copilot-cli for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. This image is for connecting SDK clients to a server, not for interactive terminal use.
Set a connection token and a GitHub token, then start the server:
export COPILOT_CONNECTION_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
docker run --rm \
  -p 127.0.0.1:4321:4321 \
  -e COPILOT_CONNECTION_TOKEN \
  -e COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN \
  ghcr.io/github/copilot-cli:latest
Set COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN in your environment before running the command. For version-pinned deployments, use a release tag instead of latest. See the container image guide for SDK connection examples, configuration, security considerations, and build instructions.
Experimental mode enables access to new features that are still in development. You can activate experimental mode by:
- Launching with the --experimental flag: copilot --experimental
- Using the /experimental slash command from within the CLI
Once activated, the setting is persisted in your config, so the --experimental flag is no longer needed on subsequent launches.
- Autopilot mode: Autopilot is a new mode (press Shift+Tab to cycle through modes), which encourages the agent to continue working until a task is completed.
Each time you submit a prompt to GitHub Copilot CLI, your monthly quota of premium requests is reduced by one. For information about premium requests, see About premium requests.
For more information about how to use the GitHub Copilot CLI, see our official documentation.
GitHub Copilot CLI supports Language Server Protocol (LSP) for enhanced code intelligence. This feature provides intelligent code features like go-to-definition, hover information, and diagnostics.
Copilot CLI does not bundle LSP servers. You need to install them separately. For example, to set up TypeScript support:
npm install -g typescript-language-server
For other languages, install the corresponding LSP server and configure it following the same pattern shown below.
LSP servers are configured through a dedicated LSP configuration file. You can configure LSP servers at the user level or repository level:
User-level configuration (applies to all projects):
Edit ~/.copilot/lsp-config.json
Repository-level configuration (applies to specific project):
Create .github/lsp.json in your repository root
Example configuration:
{
  "lspServers": {
    "typescript": {
      "command": "typescript-language-server",
      "args": ["--stdio"],
      "fileExtensions": {
        ".ts": "typescript",
        ".tsx": "typescript"
      }
    }
  }
}
Check configured LSP servers using the /lsp command in an interactive session, or view your configuration files directly.
For more information, see the changelog.
We're excited to have you join us early in the Copilot CLI journey.
We're building quickly. Expect frequent updates--please keep your client up to date for the latest features and fixes!
Your insights are invaluable! Open an issue in this repo, join Discussions, and run /feedback from the CLI to submit a confidential feedback survey!

report.summary: GitHub launches Copilot CLI, an agentic terminal tool that brings its coding agent, GitHub context, and MCP extensibility straight to developers' command lines.
report.background: AI coding assistants began as IDE autocomplete and chat panels, but through 2024-2025 the frontier moved to agentic tools that plan, edit files, run commands, and open pull requests. Anthropic's Claude Code and Google's Gemini CLI popularized the terminal as the natural home for such agents, since builds, tests, git operations, and deployments already live there. Meanwhile the Model Context Protocol (MCP) became a de facto standard for connecting agents to external tools and data. GitHub, whose Copilot was IDE-first, faced pressure to defend its position at the workflow layer it owns: repositories, issues, and pull requests. Copilot CLI answers that by reusing the same agentic harness as GitHub's cloud Copilot coding agent and shipping GitHub's MCP server by default. Notably, it defaults to Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 4.5, with GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 selectable, underscoring GitHub's model-agnostic positioning.
key_points: Terminal-native with GitHub context: you work with the agent directly in your shell without switching windows, and can query repositories, issues, and pull requests in natural language using your existing GitHub authentication. That means an agent that already understands your project's history, open work, and CI state, not just the files in the current folder.

Same agentic harness as the cloud Copilot coding agent, plus MCP extensibility: the CLI ships with GitHub's MCP server enabled by default and supports custom MCP servers, so teams can wire in internal APIs, databases, or third-party services. Capabilities include planning and executing multi-step tasks such as building, refactoring, and debugging code.

Human-in-the-loop by default: every action is previewed before execution and nothing runs without explicit approval. An experimental 'autopilot' mode, toggled via Shift+Tab or the --experimental flag, lets the agent keep working until a task completes, trading oversight for autonomy.

Broad distribution: install via curl/wget script, Homebrew, WinGet, or npm across Linux, macOS, and Windows (PowerShell 6+). A container image at ghcr.io/github/copilot-cli runs the CLI as a headless server for Copilot SDK clients, enabling scripted or embedded agent deployments rather than interactive use.

Model choice, quotas, and code intelligence: the default model is Claude Sonnet 4.5, switchable via /model to Claude Sonnet 4 or GPT-5. Each prompt consumes one premium request from your monthly quota, and organizational policy can disable access. Optional LSP support adds go-to-definition, hover, and diagnostics, but language servers must be installed and configured separately.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this intensifies the terminal-agent race and shows GitHub hedging across model providers while using its workflow ownership—repos, issues, PRs, org policy controls—as the differentiator rather than raw model quality. Defaulting to an Anthropic model signals that the durable value is the harness and distribution, not the underlying LLM. For developers, it lowers context-switching and makes agent assistance scriptable, but introduces real costs via premium request quotas, plus governance questions when agents can run shell commands; expect a learning curve in supervising rather than writing code. For regular users, the practical effect is indirect: faster bug fixes and more AI-drafted pull requests, but also more AI-generated code flowing into products, raising the stakes for review, testing, and supply-chain security. Enterprises should expect admin-level enablement decisions to gate adoption.
report.tools: Try github/copilot-cli (install via brew install copilot-cli, npm i -g @github/copilot, or the curl script), then explore MCP servers to extend it—GitHub's own MCP server is built in. Compare with Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and aider for terminal workflows. If you want code intelligence, install an LSP server such as typescript-language-server and configure ~/.copilot/lsp-config.json. Teams building automation should look at the ghcr.io/github/copilot-cli container image and the Copilot SDK for headless integrations.
